Because a sitter is a voice that stays on this side, and her mother had been crossing with only one voice to call her home, and now there were two, and one of them was blood.

Dell made Marian sit with him, the afternoon before, in the greenhouse, in the long gold light, and he told her the truth of the thing. All of it. He had never done that before, with anyone — it was not how he worked, he did not explain, he had told her that the first night — but he did it now, because he had decided she was close to the door she would not come back through, and he would not let her go through it believing anything untrue, not even a kind untruth.

He told her what it was. A thing a desert animal makes, he said — the toad, the gravest-faced creature God ever built, which spends its life underground and comes up with the rain and makes, in its own body, as a defense against the things that would eat it, the most powerful substance of its kind known on the earth. Not grown in a garden. Not cooked in a lab. Made by an animal, in the dark, under the ground, for reasons that have nothing to do with us, and we found it anyway, because we find everything.

He told her how we found it, because she asked. There was no ancient secret, he said, and she should mistrust anyone who told her there was. The people who sell this thing love to dress it in feathers, love to say the old desert peoples used it for a thousand years, and the plain honest truth is that nobody has ever found good evidence that anybody used it, for anything, until almost within living memory — until a man, an ordinary man, no shaman, a veteran and an artist who kept to himself, put out a little pamphlet about it from a town in Texas back in the nineteen-eighties, a few stapled pages, and the whole modern business grew up out of those few pages like a weed out of a crack. “It’s younger than I am,” Dell said. “People don’t like to hear that. They want it old. But I’d rather you go in knowing it’s a toad and a pamphlet than go in thinking it’s a thousand years of wisdom, because the toad and the pamphlet are the truth, and the truth is the only thing I’ve got to give you that the bucket people never get.”

He told her what it costs. That it had killed people — not often, but it had, the heart or the breath or the going-in with no one to stay on this side, and worse where someone had mixed it with the wrong medicine, because there are medicines, common ones, the kind a doctor hands a sad person every day, that turn this thing from a door into a noose. He told her that it was not a medicine, whatever anyone called it, that it cured nothing, that it had bought her not one single day and never would. And he told her the last thing, the thing that cost him to say, because it was the thing he loved: that there were fewer of the toads every year now, that the buckets and the coolers and the websites were stripping them off the land faster than the rains could bring them up, that a creature which had survived every drought the desert could throw at it for ten million years was being finished off, in his lifetime, in his own low place, by people who wanted to feel better about themselves — and that every time he opened the door for someone, even someone he loved, even her, he was spending a little of a thing the world was running out of, and he did it anyway, for her, and he wanted her to know the weight of what she was asking, down to the toad.
“Why tell me all this now,” she said, when he was done. The light was going amber over the mountains.

“Because a person should know exactly what they’re holding,” he said, “before they let go of everything to hold it. That’s all. That’s the whole of what I believe about any of it.” He looked at her the full extra half-second. “And because I think the next one’s the one, Marian. I think you’ve got one more crossing in that body and I think you know it too, and I’ll sit it with you because you’d go alone if I didn’t and that’d be worse, but I wanted you to have the truth in your hands first. The real one. The toad and the pamphlet. Not the feathers.”
The rains came back hard on the last night of August, and she went out, with Dell on one side and Dana on the other, and she walked out past the lights for the last time but one.
And this time the standing dark was close.

It had been coming nearer all summer, crossing by crossing, a column of impossible dark in all that edgeless light, and she had been afraid of it and drawn to it in the same breath, the way you are drawn to the thing you have spent your life not looking at. Now it was near. Now, as the last of her went out, as the song came apart in her hands into pure pulse and breath, as the I dissolved out of I’m here and left only the bare presence saying itself into the white — now the standing dark was so close that she could have touched it, if there had been a she, if there had been a hand, and it stopped being a column and became, the way a thing resolves when you finally let your eyes rest on it, a shape. A man’s shape. Tall. Standing easy, the way a grown man stands when he is waiting for someone and is not worried, because he knows they are coming. And the almost-nothing that was left of her, the last reed, turned fully toward it, and the standing dark — turned around.
And it had a face.

She had been afraid, all summer, of what the face would be. She had been afraid it would be the drowned face, the one she had not been let to see, the one they would not let her identify, that they had done for her, a kindness she had never forgiven because it had left her thirty years with a horror her mind supplied in the dark. She had been afraid it would be the ten-year-old’s face gone wrong.

It was none of that. It was a grown man’s face, a face in its late thirties, a kind, tired, amused, grown face — and it was his. It was unmistakably, impossibly his: she saw the ten-year-old in it the way you see the child in any grown person you have loved from the beginning, the particular set of the brow, the particular mouth that had always, even at ten, looked about to say something dry — he had been a dry child, a watcher, he would have grown up to be a watcher, she saw it all at once, the whole missing life legible in the grown face the way a whole landscape is legible from very high up — and the face looked at her, at the nothing that was her, with a tenderness so total and so adult, so much the tenderness of a grown son for an old mother, that the reed of her that was left simply broke, and she knew him, she knew him, the recognition she had felt the first night as a lurch without a name arrived now with its name, and the name was the oldest word she had, the first word she had ever taught him to read, and she would have said it if there had been a mouth left to say it with — and he smiled, the dry grown smile, and he did not speak, not yet, there were no mouths and no words yet, but he did a thing that undid her more than any word: he looked at her the way you look at someone who has come a very long way to see you, through great difficulty, when you have been waiting a long time and were beginning to think they might not come — and he let her see that he was glad. That he had been waiting. That the waiting was over.

And then she understood the whole of it, all at once, the way you understand everything in there, flat and total and without mercy: that to go to him, to close the last of the distance, to be with him the way she had come all this way to be with him — she would have to finish going out. She would have to let the last reed dissolve. There was no reaching him as Marian, because he was not somewhere a Marian could go; he was in the white, he was of it, he was the white wearing the shape of her love for him, and to be with him she would have to stop being the one who loved him and become the loving itself, edgeless, nameless, everywhere — and in that everywhere he would be hers no longer, because there would be no her for him to be the son of, there would be only the one vast thing loving itself with no parts and no names and no mothers and no sons, and she would have him completely and lose him completely in the identical instant, the way you lose a drop of water by giving it to the sea.

That was the toad’s whole truth, the thing under all the dissolution, the thing Dell could not have told her and the song had always known. She could keep him, and not reach him. Or she could reach him, and not keep him. The one thing she could not do, the one thing the white did not offer, was the thing every grieving person on earth has wanted since the first grave: to have him back, and be herself, both, in the daylight world of edges where a mother can hold one particular son.

She hung there, at the last edge, one reed from the sea, her grown son’s glad tired face in front of her, and she began to let go of the reed — and Dell’s voice came down into the white, and Dana’s came with it, the two voices, one dry and one blood, saying her name from the far side, Marian, Marian, come back, Mom, come back, Mom, please, and she felt the reed catch.
She did not go the rest of the way. That night.

She came up — torn up, the way she always came up, the self poured back into the mould like wet concrete, the time and the body and the name clamping down — and she came up weeping, and Dana was holding her, actually holding her, her grown daughter’s arms right around her on the cot, and Dell had his hand on her head, and the dog was pressed the whole length of her side, and the toads were roaring the valley full, I’m here, I’m here, who’s there, I’m here, and Marian lay in the arms of her living child and wept for her dead one, which was a thing she had not done in thirty years, had not been able to do, had built an entire still careful life around not doing, and now could not stop doing, the thirty years coming out of her all at once in the warm wet dark.
“I saw his face,” she said, when she could. “Dana. I saw his face. He’s — he grew up so kind. He would have been — he was going to be such a kind man.”

And Dana, who had flown across two states furious, who had said that’s not Jamie, that’s you, who had been right — Dana held her mother tighter and did not say it again. Because she had watched her mother’s face, out there, in the lamplight, during the fifteen minutes. She had watched the slack far-gone face of a woman under deep water meet something, and smile, and she had seen her mother’s grown face, for just a moment, wear an expression Dana had not seen on it in her entire life, not once, not in forty-three years: she had seen her mother look happy. Simply, wholly, uncomplicatedly happy, the way the very old are sometimes happy for a moment when they forget, the way Dana imagined her mother must have looked before, in the time Dana was too young to remember, the time before the wash. And whatever that was, whether it was Jamie or the grief that wore his face or the toad or the dying brain or the oldest wish there is — Dana had stopped being able to call it nothing. You do not call nothing the thing that puts that face on your mother.

“I’m not going to tell you not to go back,” Dana said, into her mother’s hair. “I spent the whole drive out here deciding not to. But I need you to hear the thing I came all this way to say, and I need you to hear it before, not after, because there might not be an after.” She was crying now too. “I was thirteen. And I lost him, and then I lost you, in the same summer, and I only ever got to grieve the one of you, because the other one was still making my lunch. So whatever you go out there to say to him —” her voice went, and came back ” — say it to me too. The goodbye. I need one too, Mom. I’ve needed one for thirty years. Don’t go all the way out to the quiet to give it to the one who can’t hear it and leave the one who can without it again.”

And Marian, in the arms of her living daughter, in the roaring dark, understood that she had been given, at the very end, the one thing the white could never give her: a second child, right here, on this side, in the world of edges, who could still be held, who had come back, who was asking — not to keep her, but to be let go of properly, which is the only thing love can do for the living when the time comes, and the hardest, and the thing Marian had never once managed, for anyone, in her whole careful holding-on of a life.
They opened the door together, the next morning.

The shut door, at the end of the hall. Marian had not been through it in thirty years. Dana had not been through it ever — she had been forbidden it at thirteen and had stopped seeing it as a door by the time she was fifteen, the way Marian had, the way the whole house had agreed to stop seeing it. And on the morning after the face, with the desert washed new and the light coming gold down the hall, the two of them stood in front of it, and Marian put her hand on the knob, and found she could not, and Dana put her hand over her mother’s hand, and the two of them turned it together.

It was just a room. That was the thing that broke them both, in the end — not that it was a shrine, because it was not a shrine, Marian had never made it a shrine, she had simply shut it, and so it was just a ten-year-old boy’s room with thirty years of dust on it, the bed unmade the way a boy leaves it, a model half-built, a library book thirty years overdue, a drawing taped to the wall going brittle and amber, the ordinary unbearable archaeology of a life that stopped on an ordinary day with no warning because the water came down the wash. And on the little desk, where she had put it the week after and never moved, was the sheet music. His song. The lullaby, in her own hand, the one she had written for him out of the three sounds of the monsoon night, with the last verse, the morning verse, the eight bars no living soul had heard — and Marian picked it up, in the gold light, in the dust, with her living daughter beside her, and she looked at the morning verse for the first time in thirty years, the verse that ended and count what the night brought home — and you, my love, and you, home to me, and she did not take her hands off it, and she did not close the lid.

“I’m going out one more time,” she said. “Tomorrow night, if the rains hold. And then I’m done, Dana, I swear it to you, one way or the other I’m done after that — and when I come back, if I come back, I’m going to sit down at that piano, and I’m going to play his song all the way to the end. For you. The part you never heard. I should have played it for you thirty years ago. I should have played it for you the day after. That’s the goodbye I owe the living one, and you’re going to get it, I promise you you’re going to get it, whatever happens out there.”
And Dana, standing in her dead brother’s room with her dying mother and thirty years of dust in the gold light, said the thing that let the book go on to its end:
“Then go get his. And come home and give me mine.”
THE CLEAR LIGHT

A hundred years ago a physician in Dublin began, almost by accident, to write down a thing the nurses had been seeing for as long as there had been nurses and had learned not to mention, because mentioning it got you a certain look.

It was this. That people, at the very end — in the last hours, sometimes the last minutes, when the body is letting go of the business of being a body — very often stop looking at the room. Their eyes go to a corner, or the foot of the bed, or the middle of the air, and they fix there, and their face changes, and they reach. They reach up, or out, with whatever is left to reach with. And if they can still speak, what they say, over and over, across every country and every century anyone has bothered to write it down in, is not that they are afraid. It is that someone has come. Someone they know. Someone, very often, who is already dead — a mother, a husband, a child gone before them — standing where no one is standing, in the plain air at the foot of the bed, come, the dying person says, with a certainty you cannot argue them out of and would be a monster to try, to help. To walk them over. To take them home.

The physician wrote them down, and then others did, carefully, the way you write down anything you cannot explain and will not pretend to — a great cross-country study, decades later, two researchers comparing the last hours of the dying in two nations on opposite sides of the earth, cultures that shared no gods and no stories, and finding the same thing in both: that the hour of death is crowded. That people do not, on the whole, go out alone. That whatever else is or is not true about any of it — and these were careful people, and they said plainly what they could not know — the dying, with a frequency no one has ever quite explained away, spend their last strength reaching for someone only they can see, and go out with a look on their faces that the ones left in the room, holding the cooling hand, describe again and again with the same helpless inadequate word: recognition. The look of a person who has seen a face they know.

Make of it what you will. The careful people did not tell you what to make of it and neither will this book. Perhaps it is the dying brain, doing the last kind thing a brain can do, furnishing the empty room with the faces we need so that we do not have to go out into the dark alone. Perhaps it is exactly what it looks like. The honest answer, the only one, is that we do not know, and that the not-knowing is not a reason to look away, because the look on the face is real whatever makes it, and the comfort is real, and the reaching is real, and a thing does not have to be explained to be true.

What every one of these accounts agrees on, across the centuries and the oceans, is the one detail this book has been walking toward since its first page: that the someone in the light is not a stranger.
that they are known.
that they have been waiting.
and that they have come, at the very last, not to keep the dying one there — but to take them home.
V. THE MORNING

The rains held, and on the first night of September she went out to the quiet one more time, with Dell on one side and Dana on the other, and this time she did not mean to come back, and this time she did.

Neither of those is quite the truth. The truth is stranger, and it is the only part of the book I am not sure how to tell, because she was only barely there to bring it back, and because what happened out past the lights that last night does not fit in the kind of sentence that has a before and an after in it. But she told Dana some of it, in the days that were left, in pieces, at the kitchen table, and Dana told Dell, and Dell told it to me the way you tell a thing you have decided to carry, and so here it is, told three times removed and still, I think, true, the way the song was true three removes from the wash.

She lay on the cot under the salvaged windows with the rain loud on the mismatched glass, and Dana held one of her hands and Dell knelt by the other, and the toads filled the valley with the only thing they ever say, and she walked out into the wings for the last time, little and scared and holding her whole self against her chest like sheet music. And this time she did not try to hold onto any of it. That was the thing she had finally learned, in a summer of practice, the thing the metronome and the shut door and the thirty held years had never let her learn: she walked to the edge of the light, and she set the music down, all of it, her name and her sixty-four years and the illness and the house and even, last, hardest, the holding-on itself — and she went out past the lights as no one at all, on purpose, the way she had been afraid her whole life she would have to and would not be able to.
And he was there.

He was there, and he was close, and this time the last reed of her did not break at the sight of him — it simply let go, the way a hand finally lets go of a thing it has gripped so long the fingers have forgotten they are gripping, and she went out the rest of the way into the white, and there was no Marian, and there was no fear, and there was no instant of going, because the instant she had been so afraid of her whole life turned out, when it came, to be the easiest thing there is, the most natural, a note at the end of a diminuendo going at last to the silence it had always been headed for, and the silence was not empty.

He was in it. Or he was it. There were no edges to say which. There were no mouths and no words, there was no one to have a mouth, but there was knowing, direct and total, the way you know a thing in a dream before anyone says it, and what she knew, first, flooding the whole white with it, was that there was nothing to forgive. That was the first thing he gave her, before anything else, because he knew it was the thing she had carried longest. Not I forgive you — that would have needed a you and a me, and there were none — but something underneath forgiveness, something forgiveness is only the daytime word for: that the account she had been keeping for thirty years, the terrible ledger of the day she did not watch him closely enough, the wash, the not-knowing-why he went out, the not-getting-to-say-goodbye, the putting-Dana-down-early, all of it, the whole thirty-year ledger — had no reader. Had never had a reader. There was no one on the other side of it keeping score, there never had been, there was only this, the white, the one thing loving itself with no parts, and in it her terrible ledger was not forgiven, it was finished, it simply stopped being a thing, the way the wash stops being a river when the water lays itself back down into the ground.
And then he showed her the life.

This is the part she could least tell and I will least try to improve. He showed her — not in pictures, there were no pictures, in the direct knowing — the whole of the life he had not been let to have, all of it present at once in the no-time the way a whole life is said to hang present at once before a drowning man: the man he would have grown into, the dry watchful kind man she had seen in the face, the work he would have done and the people he would have loved and the ordinary Tuesdays of it, forty years of ordinary Tuesdays, present, entire, not as a grief for what was lost but as a gift, as if he were saying, look, Mom, here it is, you don’t have to wonder anymore, here is the whole of what the water took, and it was good, and you can stop guarding the door on it now, because I’ve brought it out to show you, and now you’ve seen it, and now you can let it go — and under all of it, running beneath the whole white the way the brainstem runs under the bright folds of the brain, the way the wash runs under the dry, there was the song.

Her song. His song. The round, the lullaby, the three sounds of the monsoon night she had made kind for a frightened boy. It had come apart in her hands every crossing all summer, dissolved into pure pulse and breath, lost its words the way she lost her name, hush losing the hush and home losing the home and I’m here losing the here and the I — and now, at the very bottom, out of the dissolve, for the first time in thirty years, it reassembled. The words came back. And it was not her carrying them.

It was him. He was singing it. The morning verse. The eight bars no living soul had heard, the last of the song, the part she had taken her hands off of ten thousand times and closed the lid on, the morning that could not come because he was not in it — he sang it to her, in the white, in the direct knowing that was better than any voice, the whole of it, all the way to the end she had never once reached:
And when the morning comes up gold, and the wash lies down, and the singing’s through,

I’ll open your door on the washed-new day and count what the night brought home — and here, where she had always stopped, where the lid had always come down, he did not stop. He went on. He gave her the end.
— every toad to its stone, every bird to its tree, every drop of the rain to the waiting sea — and you, my love. And you. And you.
Home to me.
And she understood, then, in the instant that had no time in it, that she had had the song wrong for thirty years.

She had thought the morning verse could not be sung because its and you was a counting of who came home, and he had not come home, and so the count was broken forever and the song could not end. She had thought home to me meant the child home to the mother, the thing the wash had made impossible, the thing she could not say and so could not finish.

But he was singing it to her. That was the whole of it, the thing the toad had been carrying her toward all summer in the only language it had. Home to me was not the dead child coming home to the living mother. It was the living one being sent home. And you, my love. And you. Home. The morning comes up gold, and the wash lies down, and the night is over, and every single thing the night took hold of is let go of now, back to where it lives — the toad to its stone, the rain to the sea, and you, you most of all, you back to the house, to the morning, to the washed-new day, to the living, to the one who is still in the house waiting for you. He was not asking her to stay. He had never been waiting for her to come and join him in the quiet. He had been waiting, thirty years, for her to come close enough that he could finally send her back.

Go on, Mom, he said, in the direct knowing, with the dry grown amusement she had seen in the face, the kindness that had always, even at ten, looked about to say something true. You came all this way to learn how to let go, and you kept thinking it was me you had to let go of. It was never me. I was already gone, the easy way, the way the water goes. It was the holding-on you had to put down. And now you have. So go on. You did it. You practiced the whole thing. You’re ready. And then, because he was his mother’s son, because she had taught him that anything can be learned if you go slow enough and do it again: You’ve got one more thing to go home and play all the way through. Don’t take your hands off it this time.

And she wanted to stay. Of course she wanted to stay. The white was the easiest thing there had ever been, and he was in it, and there was no illness in it and no thirty years in it and no instant to be afraid of anymore because the instant was already behind her, and every atom of her that was not a mother wanted to dissolve the last of the way and be the loving with no parts, forever, with him.

But he had sung her home. And a mother does the thing her child asks, when the child is right, even when it is the hardest thing, especially then. So she did the one thing she had never once managed in her whole careful holding-on of a life. She let go of the thing she most wanted to keep, on purpose, in love, and she turned back toward the two voices calling her name from the far side of the light, the dry one and the blood one, Marian, Mom, Marian, come back, come home, and she went to them. She came home the way the morning comes. She left her son in the white where he had always been and always would be, and she did not lose him, because you cannot lose what you have finally, after thirty years, let go of on purpose — the holding-on was the losing, that was the last thing the toad taught her, that was the thing the song had always known — and she came up.

It nearly killed her, coming up. Dell said afterward it was the closest he had ever sat to the far edge with anyone and had them still come back. There was a long time — a minute, four minutes, a hundred years, the clock and the forever being the same thing seen from two sides of a wall — when the body on the cot did not breathe, and the dog stood up and whined, and Dana was saying Mom in a voice that was not a word anymore, and Dell had his hand flat on her chest and his mouth close to her ear saying her name, patient as the rain, a voice staying on this side.

And then she breathed. And the self came back, poured into the mould, the time and the body and the aching and the name, and it was violent and it was total and it was the last time, and she came up with her daughter’s face over hers and the rain on the glass and the toads roaring the valley full, and the first thing she said, the thing she said instead of who was that, the thing that told Dell before she said another word that it was done, that she would not be coming out to the low place again, was:
“Take me home. I have to play it for her. I promised.”
She played it the next afternoon, in the front room, in the gold light, with the shut door at the end of the hall standing open now and the dust still in the air of it.

It cost her nearly everything she had left. Dana had to help her to the bench. Her hands were not good anymore; the illness had been in them for weeks; they shook, and they were cold, and she looked at them in her lap for a moment the way she had looked at them in the white, as if they belonged to someone she had heard about once. And then she put them on the keys, and the strangest thing happened, the thing she had promised eleven frightened children every summer for thirty-six years and never once got to prove so completely herself: the hands knew the way. She had practiced this. Not the dying — the playing. Ten thousand hours at this bench, scales and scales and scales, so that one day, when the music she loved finally came and the rest of her was too frightened or too weak or too far gone to find it, the hands would already know the way. And they did. They went into the song, his song, the round made of the three sounds of the monsoon night, and they played it true, shaking and cold and dying, the first verse and the refrain and the second and the third, the whole thing Dana had grown up hearing through the wall, the whole thing that had always, always stopped at the same bar — and this time the hands did not stop. This time, when they came to the turn where the lid had always come down, they went on, into the morning verse, the eight bars no one in that house had ever heard, and Marian played the morning all the way up gold, and the wash lying down, and the counting of what the night brought home — every toad to its stone, every bird to its tree, every drop of the rain to the waiting sea — and she did not take her hands off the keys, and she played the last line, the one she had carried out of the white, the one he had sung her home with, and you, my love, and you, and you, home to me, and she let the last chord ring all the way out into the silence it had always been headed for, and she did not close the lid.

Dana stood by the piano with her hand over her mouth and heard, at forty-three, the end of the song her little brother was put to sleep with, the end her mother had withheld from the whole world for thirty years because it was the end of everything — and understood that it was not the end of everything, that it had never been, that it had always, secretly, under the grief, been a song about sending the ones you love home in the morning, and that her mother had just, finally, thirty years late and at the cost of nearly all she had left, sung her daughter home too.
That was Dana’s goodbye. The living one’s. She got it. He had made her mother promise, out in the white, and her mother had kept the promise, and it was the last full thing Marian’s hands ever did.

She died eleven days later, in the house, in the first week of the rains’ long ending, with the door at the end of the hall standing open and the metronome, which she had asked Dana to wind, going on the upright in the front room, tock . . . tock . . . tock, beating its patient time at the empty air.

It did not frighten her. That is the thing I most want you to have, out of all of it, the thing she practiced a whole summer and paid for with the last of herself to be able to give to whoever is listening: when the instant came, the great involuntary one, the letting-go she had organized sixty-four years around never having to do without rehearsal — she had rehearsed it. She knew the way. It came, the diminuendo, the note going soft and soft, the self thinning out the way it had thinned a dozen times on a cot in a greenhouse, and she did not flinch from it, did not recoil the way the old book says most people do, the way she would have, once, before the summer. She had studied the face of it until it was not a stranger. She went to it the way you go out past the lights when you have done it a thousand times — set the music down in the wings, and walked out, little and unafraid, into the thing with no edges, where the morning was already gold, and the wash was already lying down, and someone had already saved her a place, and was already, under everything, beginning to sing.
And the self did not reassemble.

That was the only mercy in it and it was a complete one. There was no coming-up this time, no violent pouring back into the mould, no time clamping down, no name. The morning she did not reach for the name was the morning she did not have to, and the room was still there, and the light came gold down the hall and into the open door at the end of it, and the little wooden arm went on beating time at the air for no one, slower now, the spring running down, tock . . . . . tock . . . . . . tock, and there was no one left in the book to be afraid, and no one left to practice, and nothing left to let go of, and the holding-on that had been a whole life was finally, gently, set down in the wings.

Dana was in the kitchen. She had got up to make coffee, because it was morning, because the living have to eat, because thirty years of her mother’s terrible competence had taught her that you make the lunch and you sort the pills and you put one foot in front of the other through the unbearable thing, and she had the cup in her hand and the light was coming up gold over the Rincons and the last of the toads were singing somewhere out past the wash, winding down with the rains, I’m here, I’m here, who’s there, fewer of them every night now, and she heard the metronome stop.

Just that. The tock she had wound that morning and stopped hearing the way you stop hearing a clock, and then the small enormous fact of its absence, the spring run all the way down, the arm come to rest.

And she stood in the kitchen with the cup in her hand and did not go in, not yet, not for a minute, because she knew, and because once she went in it would be true, and because she wanted to give her mother one more minute of the morning before it was true. And in that minute she found that she was not holding a horror. She was holding a grief — a plain, particular, Marian-shaped, Jamie-shaped grief, the bounded human kind, the kind with edges, the kind you can carry in two hands like a man carrying water, like a toad, grave-faced, out of a flood — and she understood that this was the thing her mother had gone all the way out into the quiet to be able to hand her, and had come all the way back to put in her hands, and had spent her very last full strength teaching her, at the piano, in the gold light, how to carry.

Then she set down the cup, and she went in to her mother, through the house with the open door at the end of the hall, in the washed-new morning, with the rain finally over and the ground drinking it down, and every drop of it going home to the waiting sea.
WHAT IT DID

The substance in this book is 5-MeO-DMT [five-em-ee-oh-dee-em-TEE], a tryptamine made in the glands of the Sonoran Desert toad as a defence, and found also in a few plants. Smoked, it is among the most powerful psychedelics known. This is what it did, here, to Marian, set down plainly.

Time. It ended. Not sped or slowed — ended. There was no sequence left for events to sit in, no before and after, no way to say whether four minutes or a hundred years had passed, because both are what you say from outside, and she was not outside.
The body. It went first, the way a coat comes off, sleeve by sleeve, and she did not miss it, which frightened her more than losing it would have.

The self. It dissolved. This is the whole of what the substance does and the reason it is in this series: it does not decorate the self or frighten the self or lift the self — it takes the self away entirely, the name, the memories, the one doing the looking, until there is no one there to whom anything is happening. This is called ego dissolution, and the people it happens to can rarely say more about it than that it happened, because the thing that would remember was the thing that went.

The world. There was no crowded vision, no colours, no figures, none of the furniture of the better-known doors. There was a white, a light with no edges and no source, a nothing that was not empty. People come back calling it unity, or the ocean, or God, and admitting in the same breath that all three are wrong.

The meaning. Overwhelming and un-carry-able: the flat total certainty that this was what is always there, under everything, and that one had simply never looked. And the particular cruelty this book is built on — that there is nothing to bring back from it, no souvenir, because the thing it does is take the hands that would have carried something home.
On the old strength scale that runs from nothing to plus four, her last crossing was a plus four: the rare one, the one that may never come again, and the one she did not quite come back from.
THE MAPMAKER
For Vittorio Erspamer, who found it, and for Ken Nelson, who told.
Two men, mostly, are the reason anyone knows what this toad makes, and they could not have been less alike, and neither of them ever met the other, and the series owes this page to both.

The first was a scientist. Vittorio Erspamer [vit-TOR-ee-oh er-SPAH-mer] was an Italian pharmacologist, one of the great patient chemists of the living world, the man who first identified serotonin — the brain’s own messenger of mood — years before it had that name. He spent part of his long career on the skins of toads, which are among the busiest chemical factories in nature, and somewhere in that work he put the secretions of some forty kinds of toad under his instruments and found that one of them, and only one, the big grave-faced toad of the Sonoran Desert, built in its own glands the powerful tryptamine this book is about. He was not looking for a door in the mind. He was cataloguing what toads are made of, the way a man might map a coastline with no intention of ever landing on it. But he is the one who drew the molecule’s home onto the chart, and said: here, in this animal, and nowhere else like this.

The second was not a scientist at all. His name was Ken Nelson, and for most of his life almost no one knew it, because he published the one thing he is remembered for under a made-up name, Albert Most. He was a veteran and an artist and a loner who, for more than twenty years, lived on a decommissioned missile base outside Denton, Texas. In 1981, stationed far away, he read a magazine piece about an old excavation that had turned up thousands of toad bones, and something in it caught and would not let go. He found Erspamer’s work. He understood what it meant: that out in the Sonoran Desert there was an animal carrying, in its own body, one of the most powerful substances of its kind on earth. He went to find it, and on his first trip there were no toads at all, because they were still underground, waiting for the rain. He went back after the rains came, in the early 1980s, and found one, and dried what it made, and became, as far as anyone has ever been able to establish, the first person in the modern world to deliberately do what this book describes — and then, being the kind of man he was, he wrote it down, a few stapled pages, and sent it out into the world, and the whole of what has grown up since grew out of that.

And here is the thing this page exists to say plainly, because the series promised you the truth and this is the hardest piece of it. There is no ancient tradition. People will tell you the desert peoples used this toad for a thousand years; there is no good evidence that anyone used it, ever, for anything, until Nelson dried that venom on the hood of his van. The practice is younger than most of the people doing it. That does not make it small. But it makes it honest, and honesty was the deal.

Nelson spent his later years trying to work out how to make the substance without the toad, in a laboratory, from scratch — not to sell it, but to take the pressure off the animal, because he had seen what was coming. He was right about what was coming. The toads are being stripped off the land now faster than the rain brings them up; a recent survey of the Mexican populations found several of them crashing toward nothing, hunted out for the very thing this book is about. Nelson did not live to see the worst of it. He developed Parkinson’s disease, and died in 2019, a little over a year before the world finally learned the real name of the man who had written as Albert Most. Reprints of his little pamphlet have since raised money to fight the illness that killed him.

A scientist who mapped the coast and never meant to land. A loner who landed, and told everyone, and spent the rest of his life worried about what he had started. Between the two of them, the whole truth of the thing — and not one feather on it.

GLOSSARY
agonist [AG-uh-nist] — a substance that switches a receptor on, the way a key turns a lock; the opposite of the thing that blocks it.
bufotenin [byoo-fuh-TEN-in] — a second tryptamine in the toad’s secretions, close kin to the one this book is about.
caliche [kuh-LEE-chee] — the hard, pale, cement-like crust of the desert ground, set by the long dry.
creosote [KREE-uh-soht] — the low grey desert bush that releases its clean sharp resin at the first rain; the smell most desert people mean by the smell of rain.
diminuendo [dih-min-yoo-EN-doh] — in music, a passage growing gradually softer, dying away toward silence.
estivate [ES-tih-vayt] — to pass the hot dry season asleep underground, the way other animals pass the winter; what the toad does for most of the year.
5-MeO-DMT [five-em-ee-oh-dee-em-TEE] — short for five-methoxy-dimethyltryptamine; the powerful tryptamine the
Sonoran Desert toad makes in its glands.
Incilius alvarius [in-SIL-ee-us al-VAIR-ee-us] — the scientific name of the Sonoran Desert toad, once called Bufo alvarius; the largest toad native to the United States.
monsoon [mon-SOON] — the season of hard afternoon and evening thunderstorms that breaks the desert summer, usually from July into September.
parotoid gland [puh-ROT-oyd] — the large gland behind a toad’s eye that holds its defensive secretions.
receptor [rih-SEP-ter] — a tiny lock on the surface of a brain cell that a matching molecule can open; the door the whole series is about.
saguaro [suh-WAH-roh] — the giant branching cactus of the
Sonoran Desert, the tall one with arms.
serotonin [serr-uh-TOH-nin] — the brain’s own messenger of mood; the family of molecules this toad’s substance belongs to.
Sonoran Desert [suh-NOR-un] — the hot desert of southern
Arizona and northwest Mexico, where the toad lives.
tryptamine [TRIP-tuh-meen] — the chemical family that includes serotonin and most of the classic visionary substances; the toad’s is one of them.
